lesson.title: Measuring the Spread: Variance of a Random Variable
lesson.summary: Variance measures how far the values of a random variable typically stray from its expected value, extending the ordinary variance formula to a probability distribution by weighting squared deviations by their probabilities.
lesson.body:
Knowing the expected value of a random variable tells you where its distribution is centered, but it says nothing about how spread out the possible outcomes are around that center. Variance fills that gap. In an ordinary data set, variance is computed by finding how far each value is from the mean, squaring those deviations so that negative and positive differences do not cancel each other out, and then averaging the squared deviations. Variance of a random variable applies the identical idea to a probability distribution, except each squared deviation is weighted by its probability instead of divided by a count of data points.

The formula is Var(X) equals the sum, over every possible value x, of the quantity x minus E(X), squared, times P(X = x). It is sometimes written using the symbol sigma squared with a subscript X. Squaring each deviation guarantees every term is positive, and it also has the effect of giving extra weight to values that sit far from the mean, since a large deviation becomes an even larger number once squared.

Continue with X, the number of pets owned by a randomly selected student, distribution x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1, and expected value E(X) = 1.3 from the previous chapter. Find each squared deviation from 1.3 and weight it by its probability:

(0 - 1.3)^2 = 1.69, weighted: 1.69(0.2) = 0.338
(1 - 1.3)^2 = 0.09, weighted: 0.09(0.4) = 0.036
(2 - 1.3)^2 = 0.49, weighted: 0.49(0.3) = 0.147
(3 - 1.3)^2 = 2.89, weighted: 2.89(0.1) = 0.289

Adding the weighted column: 0.338 + 0.036 + 0.147 + 0.289 = 0.81.

So Var(X) = 0.81. Notice the unit problem this creates: the original variable was measured in pets, but because every deviation was squared, the variance is technically in pets squared, a unit with no natural real world meaning. That awkwardness is exactly why variance is almost always paired with its square root, standard deviation, which converts the spread back into the original units, the subject of the next chapter.

To build intuition for what variance measures, imagine an alternate school where literally every student owns exactly 1 pet. That distribution would have P(1) = 1 and probability 0 everywhere else, so E(X) = 1 and every single deviation from the mean is 0, making Var(X) = 0. Zero variance means zero spread, everyone in the population is identical on this variable. Compare that to the real pets distribution above, with Var(X) = 0.81, which describes a population genuinely mixed across 0, 1, 2, and 3 pet owners. The larger the variance, the more the individual outcomes tend to scatter away from the expected value.
